question: You are reviewing a hypothetical Indian FMCG company. The Income Statement shows Depreciation of ₹200 Cr. On the Cash Flow Statement, what should you expect to see, and why?
before: Depreciation is a non-cash expense — it reduces Net Profit on the Income Statement (reflecting wear and tear of assets) but no actual cash leaves the company in that period. The cash already left when the asset was purchased years ago (which would have shown up as Capex under CFI back then). On the indirect method Cash Flow Statement (used by virtually all Indian companies under Ind AS), the structure is: Start with Net Profit → Add back non-cash expenses like Depreciation and Amortisation → Adjust for working capital changes → Arrive at Cash Flow from Operations. Option A confuses depreciation with capex — capex is the cash outflow, depreciation is just the accounting allocation of that prior outflow. Option C is wrong because depreciation absolutely appears, just as an add-back. Option D makes no sense — depreciation is never a cash inflow and never a financing activity. This add-back logic is one of the most tested concepts in equity research interviews — burn it into memory.
after:
Concept: Depreciation is a non-cash expense—it reduces accounting profit on the Income Statement but involves no actual cash movement in the current period. The cash outflow occurred years earlier when the asset was purchased.

Why this is correct: Under the indirect method (standard for Indian companies under Ind AS), the Cash Flow Statement starts with Net Profit and adds back all non-cash expenses to isolate actual cash generation from operations. Depreciation of ₹200 Cr appears as a ₹200 Cr add-back in the Operating Activities section because it was subtracted to arrive at Net Profit but consumed no cash.

Why the others are wrong: Option A confuses depreciation with capital expenditure—capex is the cash outflow that appears in Investing Activities when the asset is purchased, not depreciation. Option C incorrectly assumes depreciation vanishes from the Cash Flow Statement; it must appear as an add-back to reconcile profit to cash. Option D is incorrect because depreciation is neither a cash inflow nor a financing activity; financing activities concern debt and equity, not asset wear allocation.

Intuition: This add-back reveals a critical distinction in equity research—a company with high depreciation may show depressed Net Profit but stronger operating cash flow than apparent. Conversely, a low-depreciation business (or one capitalizing expenses) may flatter reported profits while understating true cash generation. Mastering the reconciliation between profit and cash flow is essential for spotting quality of earnings.
